gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Baseus PicoGo Pro AH22 (the one 100 W charger here with a tested iPhone 18 Pro AVS mode) keeps 67 W for a laptop only on port C1 in Smart mode at 20 V (67 + 30 W, Smartzone), and that every 100 W charger holding 65 W for the laptop leaves the phone port at 30-35 W, below Apple's 40 W line for iPhone 17 and its 60 W-capable AVS line for iPhone 18 Pro.
standout_why: Compared against thisusb (A2343 vs A2688), specseveryday, cadiens, computingforgeeks, techfromalex and the two Anker pages ChatGPT cited. They already carry the Anker 65 + 35 W and UGREEN 65 + 30 W tables, the 'laptop on C1 / upper port' rule, the 5 A e-marked cable rule, UGREEN's brief pause on plug-in and its Dell/Lenovo caveat; specseveryday also quotes Apple's iPhone 18 Pro AVS requirement and notes that 30 W misses the iPhone 17 line. None mentions the Baseus AH22 at all (its split, its port-position trap, its modes), none gives a measured PPS range for the Anker A2688 (thisusb and specseveryday say Anker publishes none), and none states the two-device phone-port ceiling as a general limit of 100 W chargers.
decides: It confirms the Anker A2688 and UGREEN Nexode 100W for the laptop's 65 W and adds a third qualifying row that we link: the Baseus AH22, on the condition that the laptop is on C1 and the mode is Smart or Turbo. That row rests on one named reviewer (Smartzone); techtest.org lists 45 + 45 W for C1 + C2, and I could not open Baseus's own table, so the page must name both. It also sets the phone caveat for every row: with 65 W held for the laptop, a 100 W charger cannot give an iPhone 17 its 40 W fast charge (Anker's 35 W is closest) or an iPhone 18 Pro its top AVS tier; a shopper who wants both needs a charger of about 105-125 W or more, which is outside this page's top three.
